results.name: yes_rate_drop_late_minus_early
results.description: Yes rate on the last fifth of trials (trial_index >= 360) minus the yes rate on the first fifth (trial_index < 90); a more negative observed value than the null means people grow more conservative over the session, which the stationary model fails to produce.

results.name: yes_rate_inrange_wide_sets
results.description: Yes rate for non-example targets strictly inside the [min, max] range of multi-example sets spanning at least 40; observed below the null means the model over-endorses the interior of wide example ranges (humans do not fill in broad intervals).
results.code:
# name: yes_rate_inrange_wide_sets
# description: Yes rate for non-example targets strictly inside the [min, max] range of multi-example sets spanning at least 40; observed below the null means the model over-endorses the interior of wide example ranges (humans do not fill in broad intervals).
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values
    n = (~np.isnan(sets)).sum(axis=1)
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(sets, axis=1), np.nanmax(sets, axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    member = (sets == t[:, None]).any(axis=1)
    mask = (n >= 2) & (hi - lo >= 40) & (t > lo) & (t < hi) & ~member
    if mask.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[mask].mean())

results.name: yes_rate_target_in_examples
results.description: Yes rate among trials whose target is itself one of the example numbers; observed below the null means the model is too confident that shown examples belong to the concept (humans say no more often).

results.name: yes_rate_near_outside_range
results.description: Yes rate for targets lying outside the examples' [min, max] range but within 10 of it (multi-example sets only); observed above the null means humans generalize beyond the examples' range more than the size-principle intervals predict.
results.code:
# name: yes_rate_near_outside_range
# description: Yes rate for targets lying outside the examples' [min, max] range but within 10 of it (multi-example sets only); observed above the null means humans generalize beyond the examples' range more than the size-principle intervals predict.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values
    n = (~np.isnan(sets)).sum(axis=1)
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(sets, axis=1), np.nanmax(sets, axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values
    dist = np.where(t < lo, lo - t, np.where(t > hi, t - hi, 0.0))
    mask = (dist > 0) & (dist <= 10) & (n >= 2)
    if mask.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(df["rating"].values[mask].mean())

results.name: between_participant_yes_rate_sd
results.description: Standard deviation across participants (contiguous row blocks, each starting where trial_index resets to 0) of the overall yes rate; observed above the null means individuals differ in response bias far more than the single shared-parameter model produces.

results.name: lag1_response_autocorrelation
results.description: Within-participant lag-1 correlation between consecutive yes/no responses (rows in session order, participants split where trial_index resets); observed above the null means responses are sequentially dependent (perseveration/streaks) beyond what stimulus-driven independent responding predicts.

results.name: yes_rate_far_targets
results.description: Yes rate for targets more than 40 away from the nearest end of the examples' [min, max] range; observed above the null means humans have a higher floor of far-generalization (or lapse) "yes" responses than the model.

def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values
    lo, hi = np.nanmin(sets, axis=1), np.nanmax(sets, axis=1)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).values

results.name: parity_match_effect
results.description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all share one parity, yes rate for targets of that parity minus yes rate for targets of the other parity; observed above the null means humans use parity more strongly than the model's odd/even rules allow (below means less).
results.code:
# name: parity_match_effect
# description: Among multi-example sets whose examples all share one parity, yes rate for targets of that parity minus yes rate for targets of the other parity; observed above the null means humans use parity more strongly than the model's odd/even rules allow (below means less).
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric, errors="coerce").values
    valid = ~np.isnan(sets)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    par = np.where(valid, np.mod(np.nan_to_num(sets), 2), np.nan)
    n_odd = np.nansum(par, axis=1)
    same = (n >= 2) & ((n_odd == 0) | (n_odd == n))
    set_par = (n_odd > 0).astype(int)
    tpar = df["target"].astype(int).values % 2
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).values
    m1 = same & (tpar == set_par)
    m0 = same & (tpar != set_par)
    if m1.sum() == 0 or m0.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[m1].mean() - r[m0].mean())
